passage: For about a month last year I answered everything in single words. "Fine." "Okay." "Nothing." I sat with my phone at meals and stared at it even when nothing was on the screen. Nobody could tell why, and honestly neither could I. I was tired, because I'd been sleeping badly, and I was hurt about a fight with my friend Dev, and mostly I didn't want to talk about it. My sister Leela didn't accuse me of being rude. She put a plate of mango beside me and said, "No need to talk, I'm just here." She did that for weeks. One evening, out of nowhere, I told her everything. She only said "thank you for telling me." - Chetan

qa.q: What did Chetan sit with at meals?
qa.a: Chetan sat with a phone at meals.

qa.q: What might Chetan have been feeling during that month?
qa.a: Chetan felt tired and hurt about the fight with Dev and didn't want to talk, so the single words covered several feelings at once.

qa.q: What did Leela do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't accuse Chetan, stayed nearby and checked in patiently over weeks, so Chetan could talk when ready.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: She may have felt worried and unsure whether her quiet care was working, but she kept showing up.

grounding: A teen who withdraws, answers in single words and stares at a screen has several causes, and patient check-ins help.

passage: Form tutor's note. Over the last three weeks Jeevan's behaviour in class has changed. He arrives late, answers in single words, and stares at his phone under the desk in the breaks instead of sitting with his friends. He isn't rude and he isn't in trouble; he just seems far away. I don't know the reason. It could be tiredness, a problem at home, hurt feelings with a friend or simply a dull stretch. I haven't confronted him. Instead I say good morning each day and ask one easy question, such as how football went. Yesterday he answered with a full sentence. I'll keep checking in over the coming weeks. - Anirban

qa.q: How long has Jeevan's behaviour been different?
qa.a: It has changed over the last three weeks.

qa.q: What might Jeevan be feeling behind his single words and phone use?
qa.a: It could be tiredness, worry about something at home, hurt with a friend or plain boredom, and Anirban admits not knowing which.

qa.q: Why did Anirban choose easy daily questions over confronting Jeevan?
qa.a: Detachment has many causes, so accusing him could make him withdraw further, while patient small check-ins keep the door open.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel about Jeevan's change?
qa.a: Anirban seems concerned but careful, admitting not knowing the reason and choosing small daily check-ins over confronting him.

grounding: A teen who withdraws and stares at a screen may be tired, hurt or bored, and patient check-ins are better than accusations.

passage:
Thursday
Vinita didi has been weird for two weeks. She comes home, says "hmm" to everything, and stares at her phone on the bed. Yesterday I asked if she wanted to play carrom and she said "no" without even looking up.
Mummy said, "She's just being moody." Papa said, "Too much phone."
I didn't want to accuse her. So I kept checking, small. Monday I left her a samosa. Tuesday I sat on her bed for five minutes and said nothing. Wednesday I asked, "Tired or sad?"
Today she finally said, "Tired. The college bus takes two hours now because of the road work. And I'm scared about the internal exam."
She wasn't angry with us. She was exhausted.
I told Mummy. Mummy now keeps dinner hot and doesn't ask questions at the door.
- Harish

qa.q: How long does the college bus take now?
qa.a: Two hours, because of the road work.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling behind the single-word answers?
qa.a: Vinita was exhausted from the long bus ride and anxious about the internal exam, not angry with the family.

qa.q: What made Harish's approach work?
qa.a: Small, patient check-ins over several days, without accusing, gave Vinita space until she was ready to talk.

qa.q: How did Mummy and Papa first read Vinita's detachment?
qa.a: Mummy read it as moodiness and Papa as too much phone, both guessing wrong.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager's withdrawal having a hidden cause, and patient check-ins over time working better than accusations.

passage:
In the small town of Nabha, Shankar noticed that his daughter Hansa had gone quiet. After school she lay on the charpai with her phone, scrolling without really looking. When he asked about her day, she said, "Fine." Dinner? "Okay." Tuition? "Hmm."
His brother said, "She's become rude. Take the phone away."
Shankar didn't. Instead, every evening he sat on the step near the charpai with his tea, not asking anything. Some days he mentioned something small: the neighbour's new calf, the rain.
On the fourth evening, Hansa put the phone down. "Papa, Simran moved to Ludhiana. Her father got transferred. She didn't even tell me until the day before."
"You're hurt."
"Very."
Shankar nodded. "Tell me about her."
Hansa talked until the tea went cold.

qa.q: Where did Simran move?
qa.a: To Ludhiana.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling underneath her one-word answers?
qa.a: Hansa was hurt and sad that her friend Simran had moved away and told her only the day before.

qa.q: What did Shankar do instead of taking the phone away?
qa.a: He sat near her every evening with tea, without asking or accusing, until she was ready to talk.

qa.q: How did Shankar's brother read Hansa's detachment?
qa.a: He read it as rudeness and wanted to punish her by taking the phone.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager's withdrawal coming from hurt, and patient check-ins over time working better than accusations.

passage: In their Toronto apartment, dinner had become a one-word show. "How was school, Xin?" "Fine." "Swimming?" "Fine." Then the phone came out, and Xin's eyes stayed on it until the plates were cleared. Ivan, who had married Xin's mother two years before, felt the old urge to say "You're being rude," and swallowed it. He didn't know if Xin was tired, sad, private or just bored with him. So he tried something slower. Every evening he knocked once, said, "Making hot chocolate, want one?" and left it at that. Most nights the answer was "No." On the ninth night it was "Okay." On the twelfth, Xin sat on the kitchen stool while the milk heated and said, without looking up, "Morning practice is at five now. And everyone in Vancouver has stopped replying." Ivan nodded, stirred, and didn't lecture. "That's a lot at once," he said. Xin took the mug. "Yeah."

qa.q: What time is morning practice now?
qa.a: Morning practice is at five now.

qa.q: What might Xin have been feeling behind the one-word answers?
qa.a: Xin was likely exhausted from the early practice and lonely, hurt that old friends in Vancouver had stopped replying; from outside it could have looked like boredom or rudeness.

qa.q: Why did the hot chocolate routine work better than calling Xin rude?
qa.a: It offered a low-pressure chance to connect every evening without accusation, so after twelve nights Xin was ready to say what was going on.

qa.q: What was dinner like for Ivan during those weeks?
qa.a: Ivan felt shut out and tempted to scold, unsure whether the silence was about him, but chose patience instead.

grounding: It shows a teenager's withdrawal and single-word answers having unclear causes, and patient check-ins over time working better than accusations.
